newsitem.title: UK: Burton highlights department store revival.
newsitem.headline: Burton highlights department store revival.

text.p: Burton Group Plc on Tuesday became the latest retailer to cash in on Britain's department store boom by announcing plans to float off its highly profitable Debenhams chain.

The department store, a nineteenth century creation, had frequently been written off as a retail dinosaur, but heavy investment by leading players in recent years has given this style of retailing a new lease of life.

Debenhams, with 92 outlets around Britain, has consistently outperformed Burton's individual fashion shops, which include Dorothy Perkins and Top Shop. Last year it turned in profits of 103 million pounds ($173 million), almost double that of the fashion multiples business.

Debenhams' sparkling performance illustrates the revival of the department store as a popular place to shop, and has confounded predictions that these stores, with their huge range of merchandise, were old fashioned and on their way out.

In fact department stores now make up one of the fastest growing retail sectors in Britain, expected to deliver combined sales growth of almost 10 percent this year, according to analysts' predictions.

Millions of pounds spent on smartening up the shops by House of Fraser Plc, Burton and Selfridges, part of Sears Plc, is beginning to pay off and analysts believe there will be more growth over the medium term.

Under-investment had left many of the stores with a dowdy image, prompting industry watchers to predict they would be unable to compete with trendier, specialist shops springing up in the early 1990s.

"Many stores suffered from under-investment in the 1970s and 1980s, but they are now enjoying something of a renaissance," said retail analysts Corporate Intelligence. "They are regarded as essential "anchors" for new shopping developments."
The stores have benefited from the retail upturn over the past 12 months, but money spent on refurbishment has contributed to their success.

Market leader John Lewis, Debenhams and House of Fraser are all planning to open new stores over the next four years. But over the longer term expansion will be limited by a crackdown on out-of-town shopping developments.

The main emphasis will be on improving returns from existing outlets as well as trying to entice younger shoppers with high fashion concessions, according to Corporate Intelligence's report on the sector, published at the end of June.
"Things are set reasonably fair for the medium term," said Robert Clark at Corporate Intelligence.
Burton's planned demerger follows rival Sears decision to spin off its star profit earner Selfridges and the successful float of Harvey Nichols by its Hong Kong parent Dickson Concepts last year.

The top 50 firms operate a total of 364 outlet across the country, although around 20 of these are specialists, focusing on furniture or household goods, rather than the full range, which can cover anything from food to designer clothes. ($ = 0.594 British Pounds)
